subject: Quantitative Aptitude
topic: Percentage Applications — Reverse %, % Change, Marks, Population and Trade Discounts (W13 B1)

questions.stem: A number is increased by 20% and then the result is decreased by 20%. What is the net percentage change?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Let original = 100. After 20% up: 120. After 20% down: 120 × 0.8 = 96. Net = −4%. SHORTCUT (memorise this): When the same percentage P is applied as increase then decrease, NET = −P²/100 loss = −20²/100 = −4%. This formula works for any pair of equal % changes of opposite sign. PAPER-SETTER TRAP: Students choose 0% (cancel intuition) or 2% (halve the %). Neither is right — it's always a NET LOSS because the base for the decrease is larger.

questions.stem: In an election between two candidates, A got 40% of votes and B got the rest. If B got 1,200 more votes than A, what was the total number of votes?
questions.explanation: B is correct. A = 40%, B = 60%. Difference = B−A = 20% = 1,200 votes. Total = 1,200/0.20 = 6,000. SHORTCUT: % difference × Total = actual difference → 20% × T = 1,200 → T = 6,000. Verify: A = 2,400; B = 3,600; B−A = 1,200 ✓. Trap: 4,800 = 0.40×total only (not total); 7,200 = 1,200×6 (wrong multiplication).

questions.stem: If petrol price increases by 25%, by what percentage must consumption be reduced so that expenditure remains unchanged?
questions.explanation: B is correct. SHORTCUT: Required reduction % = P/(100+P) × 100 = 25/125 × 100 = 20%. Proof: Old price=100, new price=125. If old consumption=1 unit (expenditure=100), new consumption = 100/125 = 0.8 units. Reduction = 0.2/1 = 20%. This formula is one of the SSC paper-setter's most-tested percentage shortcuts. Trap: 25% = naive answer (reduce by same amount as increase); wrong because the base for reduction is the NEW (higher) price.

questions.stem: A student scored 30% marks and failed by 15 marks. Another student scored 45% marks and passed by 30 marks. Find the passing marks as a percentage of total marks.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Let total marks = T, passing marks = P. From student 1: 0.30T + 15 = P. From student 2: 0.45T − 30 = P. Setting equal: 0.30T + 15 = 0.45T − 30 → 45 = 0.15T → T = 300. P = 0.30(300)+15 = 105. Passing % = 105/300 × 100 = 35%. SHORTCUT: The gap between 45% and 30% = 15% of T = 45 marks (15+30) → T=300. Trap: 33% = approximate (not exact); 40% = wrong equation setup.

questions.stem: A's income is 20% more than B's income. By what percentage is B's income less than A's income?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Let B = 100, so A = 120 (20% more). B is less than A by: (120−100)/120 × 100 = 20/120 × 100 = 16⅔%. SHORTCUT: If X is r% more than Y, then Y is r/(100+r) × 100 % less than X = 20/120 × 100 = 16⅔%. PAPER-SETTER TRAP: Many students answer 20% (same percentage). The key insight: 'A is 20% more than B' uses B as base; 'B is X% less than A' uses A as the new base. The base changed, so the percentage changes. 16⅔% ≠ 20%.

questions.stem: A town's population is 50,000. It increases by 10% in the first year and decreases by 10% in the second year. What is the population after 2 years?
questions.explanation: B is correct. Year 1: 50,000 × 1.10 = 55,000. Year 2: 55,000 × 0.90 = 49,500. SHORTCUT: same % up/down → loss = P²/100 = 10²/100 = 1% of 50,000 = 500 loss → 49,500. TRAP: 50,000 = '10% up and 10% down cancel' (classic wrong intuition); 49,000 = 10% of 50,000 taken twice (wrong base).

questions.stem: A shopkeeper marks goods 40% above cost price and gives a discount of 15% on the marked price. What is the profit percentage?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Let CP = 100. MP = 140 (40% above CP). SP = 140 × 0.85 = 119 (15% discount on MP). Profit = SP−CP = 119−100 = 19%. Profit % = 19%. SHORTCUT: Net % = (1 + markup)(1 − discount) − 1 = 1.40 × 0.85 − 1 = 1.19 − 1 = 19%. Trap: 25% = 40−15 (wrong: cannot simply subtract percentages when bases differ); 17% = 40−15−8 (wrong chain).

questions.stem: One number is 20% more than another. If their sum is 198, what is the larger number?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Let smaller = y, larger = 1.2y. Sum: y + 1.2y = 198 → 2.2y = 198 → y = 90. Larger = 1.2 × 90 = 108. Verify: 90 + 108 = 198 ✓; 108/90 = 1.2 = 20% more ✓. SHORTCUT: sum = 198 = 2.2 units → 1 unit = 90 → larger = 1.2 units = 108. Trap: 99 = 198/2 (wrong; ignores the 20% difference); 104 = 90+14 (miscalculates 20% of 90 = 18, not 14).

questions.stem: In a class, 70% passed in English and 65% passed in Maths. If 10% failed in both subjects, what percentage passed in both?
questions.explanation: C is correct. Failed in both = 10% → Passed in at least one = 90%. Using inclusion-exclusion: P(E∪M) = P(E)+P(M)−P(E∩M) → 90 = 70+65−P(both) → P(both) = 135−90 = 45%. Verify: passed only English = 70−45=25%; passed only Maths = 65−45=20%; passed both = 45%; failed both = 10%; total = 25+20+45+10=100% ✓. TRAP: 35% = 70+65−100 (wrong denominator reasoning); 55% = 70+65−80 (wrong P(union)).

questions.stem: When the price of sugar falls by 20%, a person can buy 4 kg more for Rs.800. Find the original price of sugar per kg.
questions.explanation: C is correct. Let original price = p per kg. Original quantity = 800/p. New price = 0.8p. New quantity = 800/0.8p = 1000/p. Extra quantity = 1000/p − 800/p = 200/p = 4 → p = 50. Verify: original = Rs.50/kg → 16 kg for Rs.800; new price = Rs.40/kg → 20 kg for Rs.800; extra = 4 kg ✓. SHORTCUT: % price fall = 20%; extra amount purchasable from same money = 20/80 = 25% more; 25% of original qty = 4 → original qty = 16 → original price = 800/16 = Rs.50.
